cards.title: Decision complexity of weak Presburger arithmetic
cards.formal: Historical question, resolved: does removing order from Presburger arithmetic over the integers lower its decision complexity? The input is a closed first-order formula built from integer linear equalities, Boolean connectives and integer quantifiers. The task is to decide its truth in Z. There is no bound on the number of variables or quantifier alternations. Coefficients and constants are binary encoded. The 2022 result gives weak Presburger arithmetic the same STA(*, 2^{2^{n^{O(1)}}}, O(n)) completeness classification as full Presburger arithmetic, where n is input length.
cards.why: Separates expressive weakness from algorithmic simplicity in a basic decidable arithmetic theory used to describe integer constraints.
cards.status_note: Matched the integer domain, binary encoding and unrestricted quantified decision task to the MFCS 2022 result, whose abstract explicitly identifies and answers this question. Read its complexity definitions, Theorems 1 and 7 and relevant reductions, and checked the March 2026 journal corroboration. No independent proof audit is claimed.

cards.definitions: An atomic formula has the form a₁x₁+⋯+aₖxₖ=b, with aᵢ,b∈Z. Formulas are finite syntax trees formed using negation, conjunction, disjunction, and quantifiers ∃x and ∀x; a closed formula has no free variables. Quantifiers range over all positive, zero and negative integers. Coefficients multiply variables only by constants: products of two variables are unavailable. The comparison theory, full Presburger arithmetic, additionally permits linear inequalities. The input length counts the syntax and binary representations of all integers. STA(*,t(n),a(n)) denotes languages decided by an alternating Turing machine whose every computation path has at most t(n) steps and a(n) changes between existential and universal states; * imposes no separate space restriction. An existential configuration accepts if some successor accepts and a universal configuration accepts if every successor accepts. Here the time bound is doubly exponential in a polynomial of n and the alternation bound is linear in n; the notation allows fixed constants and a fixed polynomial depending on the deciding machine. The stated classification is an alternating complexity classification, not a claimed matching deterministic running-time formula.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine whether the order-free theory has the same decision-complexity classification as the ordered theory. The published lower bound already holds for positive weak arithmetic and its Horn fragment; containment in full Presburger arithmetic supplies the matching upper classification. This resolves the source question without asserting that arbitrary ordered formulas have equivalent order-free definitions.

context_blocks.title: Decision complexity and definability are different
context_blocks.text: The 2020 paper primarily asks which sets described using order can also be described without it. Its concluding motivation is a separate question about deciding the truth of arbitrary order-free sentences. A loss of expressive power alone does not imply an easier decision problem.

context_blocks.title: The integer domain is essential
context_blocks.text: The source uses all of Z. Restricting to nonnegative integers changes the definability of order, so that alteration would obscure the comparison the authors intended. Binary coefficients are also part of the source model.

context_blocks.title: A direct published resolution
context_blocks.text: Chistikov, Haase, Hadizadeh and Mansutti explicitly settle the longstanding comparison in 2022. Even the positive fragment, using ∧, ∨, ∃ and ∀ without negation, has the required hardness. Weak arithmetic therefore retains the ordered theory’s worst-case classification.

context_blocks.title: Later tractable fragments do not reopen this question
context_blocks.text: The March 2026 LMCS article cites the 2022 classification for unrestricted weak arithmetic while proving tractability for particular bounded-negation syntaxes. Restrictions on the available connective basis and quantifiers matter when comparing such fragments.

cards.context:
The 2020 paper primarily asks which sets described using order can also be described without it. Its concluding motivation is a separate question about deciding the truth of arbitrary order-free sentences. A loss of expressive power alone does not imply an easier decision problem.

The source uses all of Z. Restricting to nonnegative integers changes the definability of order, so that alteration would obscure the comparison the authors intended. Binary coefficients are also part of the source model.

Chistikov, Haase, Hadizadeh and Mansutti explicitly settle the longstanding comparison in 2022. Even the positive fragment, using ∧, ∨, ∃ and ∀ without negation, has the required hardness. Weak arithmetic therefore retains the ordered theory’s worst-case classification.

The March 2026 LMCS article cites the 2022 classification for unrestricted weak arithmetic while proving tractability for particular bounded-negation syntaxes. Restrictions on the available connective basis and quantifiers matter when comparing such fragments.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
